status: PRE-FILING / STRESS-TESTED — NO COMPLAINT. September 18 Carrillo/Vons/Asurint review materially narrows the viable vendor theories. First Advantage's furnishing of registry information and transmission of employer notices do not, standing alone, establish §290.46 or FCRA/ICRAA liability.
key_facts: First Advantage (fadv.com) is the background-screening vendor that ran the pre-employment background check underlying both Matter 25 (Newanforbi v. Federal Express Corporation) and Matter 26 (Newanforbi v. United Parcel Service, Inc.), and it is First Advantage — not the employer — that generated and transmitted every notice in both adverse-action sequences under its own letterhead (DoNotReply@fadv.com). A third First Advantage employment screen is now running for TaskUs (Matter 40): Profile Advantage invite Sep. 14, 2026 from do_not_reply@fadv.com; expected report format similar if not identical to the 25/26 product. That sequence has not yet produced a report or adverse notice. For UPS: Pre Adverse Action Notification, July 22, 2024, 9:57 AM, followed by reminder notices July 23 and July 27, 2024, and a Final Adverse Action Notification July 31, 2024, 9:57 AM. For FedEx: Pre-Adverse Employment Action Notice, March 10, 2025, 1:44 PM, a duplicate notice March 11, 2025 to a second email address, five further reminder notices between March 11 and March 16, 2025, and a final Adverse Employment Action Notice March 19, 2025, 1:47 PM. Both sequences follow an identical template and cadence roughly eight months apart, and both are alleged (on information and belief, per Matters 25/26) to have disclosed Plaintiff's Megan's Law registry status — information Penal Code § 290.46(j)(2)(E) categorically bars from employment use — to the requesting employer. Unlike Matter 29 (Amazon/Accurate Background) and the abandoned Matter 23 (Macy's/HireRight), where the vendor was named alongside the employer in a single action, First Advantage was never joined as a defendant in either Matter 25 or Matter 26, despite generating the registry-flagged report in both.
procedural_status: Do not file until a vendor-specific duty breach is identified. Obtain the underlying First Advantage reports, employer certifications under 15 U.S.C. §1681b(b)(1), master services agreements / delegated adverse-action terms, adjudication and override logs, §1681k notices or strict-procedure materials, and any accuracy/dispute record. Mendoza v. ADP Screening, 182 Cal.App.4th 1644 (2010), bars treating a CRA's mere access/compilation/republication of Megan's Law information as §290.46 'use' and rejects an ICRAA §1786.20(c) theory based on treating the Megan's Law restriction as an equal-employment-opportunity law. Federal First Advantage cases (Muir/Frazier/Williams) also caution that employer-defined CRA adjudication and notice automation do not automatically make the CRA the adverse-action decisionmaker.
damages: NOT VALUATION-READY after the September 18 stress test. Do not model employer wage/emotional-distress injury again here. Any recoverable Matter 31 value must attach to a proven First Advantage-specific statutory violation (for example an actionable certification, accuracy, §1681k, reinvestigation, or delegated-duty breach) and avoid double recovery with Matters 25/26/40.
risk: HIGH until vendor-specific proof exists. Direct §290.46 liability is presumptively weak under Mendoza if First Advantage merely reports registry information. ICRAA §1786.20(c) is directly vulnerable because Mendoza rejected the premise that Megan's Law is an 'equal employment opportunity law or regulation.' FCRA §1681b(b)(1)(A)(ii) uses materially similar language, so Carrillo's knowledge theory should not be assumed viable merely because an employer later acts unlawfully; obtain the actual employer certification first. §1681e(b) requires an accuracy/material-misleadingness problem, not merely accurate information that an employer allegedly could not lawfully use. §1681k is a more natural vendor-side track if contemporaneous notice or strict completeness/currentness procedures failed. Notice letters on First Advantage letterhead prove workflow involvement, not final hiring authority. Stronger only if discovery shows First Advantage independently set disqualifying criteria, had delegated final decision authority, furnished inaccurate/misleading data, lacked a valid certification/permissible purpose, or violated a distinct CRA duty.
